tldr: By separating latent memory (reasoning about "what to do" from past experience) from perception (determining "how to act" from the current view), this research achieves both high success rates and fast inference in robotic manipulation tasks requiring long-horizon memory.
hero_caption: Summary of ActMem's overall design philosophy and performance. (a) Drawing inspiration from cognitive science, it separates "what to do (memory)" from past experience and "how to act (perception)" from the current visual appearance. (b) It implements this decoupling within a VLA model via Latent Memory CoT and Perception Attention. (c) It significantly outperforms existing methods across benchmarks.
overview:
When a robot needs to retrieve a block hidden under a cup or pull a specific number of tissues from a box, the correct action cannot be determined solely from the current camera view. The block is occluded, and the current single frame does not reveal how many tissues have already been pulled. Existing memory-augmented VLA (Vision-Language-Action) models either store past images in a memory bank for retrieval or pack long video histories into the same context alongside current observations. However, the former struggles to infer what past context implies, while the latter allows long histories to crowd out fine-grained current perceptual details.

To tackle this, the authors drew inspiration from a cognitive science principle: memory reconstructs past experience to decide what to do, while perception guides how to act based on current conditions. Instead of storing past frames as-is, the model infers current subtasks from the full interaction history and passes the hidden states formed during this inference—termed Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought (Memory CoT)—to an action expert. At the same time, dedicated Perception Attention provides direct access to current image features, decoupling memory reasoning from perceptual grounding.

Evaluated on the RoboMemArena and MIKASA-Robo simulator environments, as well as four real-world dual-arm manipulation tasks, ActMem substantially outperformed existing memory-augmented VLAs. Furthermore, an efficient inference scheme that reuses past computations allows fast execution—under 0.6 seconds per decision even with long histories.
contributions: Proposed a new VLA architecture that decouples latent reasoning over history from current visual grounding, grounded in the cognitive science principle of separating memory and perception.

Introduced Latent Memory CoT, extracting hidden states formed while inferring subtasks from timestamped video history to convey context beyond text (such as progress and repetition count) to the action expert.
Designed Efficient Memory CoT Inference, strictly reusing prior inference results and KV caches to achieve 0.33–0.52 second decision times under long histories without altering output precision.
Demonstrated superior performance over state-of-the-art baselines across simulator benchmarks (RoboMemArena, MIKASA-Robo) and diverse real-world robot memory tasks.

sections.heading: Decoupling "what to do" from "how to act": A new balance between memory and perception
sections.summary: In memory-dependent tasks where current images are insufficient, conventional VLAs faced a trade-off between failing to reason over past history or crowding out current perception. Inspired by cognitive science, this work proposes ActMem, separating latent memory for inferring what to do from perception for guiding how to act.
sections.details:
While VLAs are gaining attention as general foundation models for robotics, most take only current camera observations as input. Consequently, they fail on tasks where past events leave no perceptual trace in the current scene. For example, if blocks are hidden under cups and shuffled, all cups look identical, making it impossible to know which cup to lift from the latest frame alone.

To address this, recent approaches store and retrieve past observation frames or feed the full video history directly into prompts. However, retrieval methods merely collect past images, forcing the action model to figure out what that history implies from scratch. Conversely, feeding long histories into a shared context causes historical tokens to crowd out fine-grained wrist-camera visual details, degrading precise manipulation.

The authors' key insight is that what robots need for decision-making is not past images themselves, but the underlying semantics inferred from history, such as task progress or repetition counts. In tissue-pulling, for example, the number of extracted sheets cannot be seen in any single image; it must be deduced from the temporal flow of video.

In cognitive science, the memory system (which reconstructs the past to decide what to do) and the perceptual system (which leverages current sensory input to guide how to act) are treated as distinct systems. Following this principle, ActMem uses a VLM (Vision-Language Model) backbone to infer subtasks from history, passes its hidden states as Latent Memory CoT to an action expert, and employs Perception Attention to grant direct access to detailed current image features.

sections.heading: How prior VLAs tackled memory
sections.summary: Recent VLA models excel at generating continuous actions, but their memory handling has remained limited to observation accumulation and retrieval, lacking semantic reasoning over history. Hierarchical methods pass subtasks only as text, discarding rich contextual nuances.
sections.details:
VLA models for robotics have rapidly evolved from autoregressive generation of discrete tokens toward continuous trajectory generation using diffusion or flow-matching action experts. Yet, most still depend solely on the current observation.

Prior memory-oriented studies proposed storing past frames in memory banks or retrieving task-relevant keyframes. However, these methods deliver raw images or compressed visual tokens directly to downstream action modules, burdening the action expert with interpreting what the history implies from scratch.

Hierarchical methods generate high-level language subtasks to guide action models, but passing subtasks purely as text strings strips away granular progress and task nuances during tokenization. Furthermore, even recent methods that take full video histories as input (such as SimpleMemVLA) cause memory reasoning and current perception to compete within the same context, diminishing dexterity in long-horizon tasks. ActMem resolves these issues by passing latent reasoning states while preserving an independent pathway for the current visual observation.

sections.heading: How ActMem works: Integrating Latent Memory CoT and Perception Attention
sections.summary: The backbone VLM infers the current subtask from video history and extracts the final-layer hidden states as Latent Memory CoT. The action expert receives this context while incorporating detailed current image features via Perception Attention to generate continuous trajectories.
sections.details:
ActMem's architecture consists of a pretrained VLM backbone (Qwen3-VL) and a flow-matching action expert (DiT: Diffusion Transformer).

### 3.1 Problem Formulation and Overview
At each decision step $t$, the robot receives a task instruction $g$, a timestamped history of observations $\mathcal{H}_t$, a current wrist-camera observation $o_t$, and proprioceptive states (joint positions, etc.) $s_t$, predicting a continuous action chunk $A_t = (a_{t+1}, \dots, a_{t+H})$ over horizon $H$.

### 3.2 Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought (Memory CoT)
First, the timestamped video $V_t$ from the head camera, the current wrist image $w_t$, and instruction $g$ are fed into the backbone. The backbone autoregressively predicts the current subtask string $\ell_t$. Crucially, instead of using the raw text string, the final-layer hidden states $C_t$ corresponding to the subtask string are extracted as the Latent Memory CoT. Under causal masking, these hidden states distill the reasoning over the full interaction history.

### 3.3 Perception Attention for Action Generation
While subtask hidden states $C_t$ capture the high-level policy of "what to do", millimeter-level manipulation demands fine visual cues from the current view. Therefore, current wrist-camera visual tokens $P_t$ encoded by the backbone are injected directly into specific layers (layers 3, 7, 11, and 15 out of 16) of the action expert using gated cross-attention (Perception Attention). Gating coefficients $\alpha_l$ are initialized to 0, ensuring training stability early on while progressively incorporating fine perceptual details.

### 3.4 Policy Learning and Fast Inference
During training, the entire network is optimized end-to-end with a multitask loss combining cross-entropy for subtasks and flow-matching loss for action generation. To prevent latency growth during deployment, the authors developed Efficient Memory CoT Inference. Recognizing that consecutive decision steps differ by only a few video frames and subtasks often stay identical, past image features and KV caches are strictly reused. By treating the previous subtask as a draft and verifying it in a single parallel forward pass, computation time is cut by more than half while producing outputs mathematically identical to standard inference.

sections.heading: Validation in simulation and real-world: High success rates and inference efficiency
sections.summary: Evaluations across RoboMemArena, MIKASA-Robo, and four real-world robotic tasks showed ActMem significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Ablations confirmed both Latent Memory CoT and Perception Attention are indispensable.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Simulations used RoboMemArena (26 long-horizon memory tasks) and MIKASA-Robo (5 tasks). Key metrics included Task Success Rate (TSR), measuring full completion, and Completion Success Rate (CSR), measuring completed task stages. Real-world experiments used a dual-arm mobile robot across exogenous memory (searching behind occluders), endogenous memory (tracking drawer exploration history), and traceless memory (counting tissue pulls) across 4 tasks.

### 4.2 Simulation Results
On RoboMemArena, ActMem achieved 71.1% TSR and 80.8% CSR, surpassing the strongest baseline, SimpleMemVLA (63.6% TSR, 72.1% CSR), by 7.5 and 8.7 percentage points, respectively. Improvements were particularly pronounced in "Occlusion" and "Sequence" tasks that heavily depend on past events. On MIKASA-Robo, it recorded a 73.8% average success rate, ranking highest among all evaluated methods.

### 4.3 Real-World Robot Experiments
In real-robot evaluations (40 trials per task), ActMem attained a 68.8% average success rate, significantly ahead of SimpleMemVLA (58.8%) and MemoryVLA (55.0%). It reached 75% on external occlusion tasks ("cups and blocks", "scissor retrieval") and 65% on "tissue pull counting".

### 4.4 Ablations and Analysis
Ablation experiments on RoboMemArena (Table 3) revealed key findings:
- Completely removing video history dropped TSR from 52.3% to 17.7%, and keeping only the most recent 10 seconds yielded just 31.2%, proving long-context retention is crucial.
- Replacing Latent Memory CoT with only subtask word embeddings dropped TSR to 40.4%, confirming that contextual hidden states hold vital information beyond discrete text.
- Omitting Perception Attention dropped TSR to 47.7%, demonstrating the necessity of direct grounding in current visual details.

### 4.5 What Does Latent Memory CoT Retain?
In a task requiring pouring wine twice, feature representations after the first and second pours were compared (Figure 5a). While input image features had a cosine similarity of 0.99 (virtually indistinguishable), Latent Memory CoT features showed a similarity of only 0.22, clearly separating the states. Even when teacher-forcing the identical subtask text string for both, similarity remained low at 0.25, confirming the hidden states intrinsically track progress counts.

### 4.6 Inference Speed
With the efficient inference scheme, decision latency was capped at 0.52 seconds (versus 1.42 seconds for standard inference) even with 90 to 126 history frames, maintaining practical control rates.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook
sections.summary: ActMem achieves high accuracy and speed in memory-intensive robotic manipulation by decoupling latent memory reasoning from perceptual grounding. A remaining challenge is selective retention of past frames over ultra-long horizons spanning tens of minutes.
sections.details:
ActMem provides an in-context memory framework that clearly separates memory reasoning from perceptual grounding within a single VLM backbone. The hidden states inferred from interaction history (Latent Memory CoT) capture subtask progress not expressed in text, while Perception Attention grounds precise hand actions. It set new state-of-the-art benchmarks in both simulation and real-world tasks.

A limitation of the current implementation is that all sampled historical frames are maintained in context. Although KV cache reuse curbs compute, attention complexity grows with episode length, gradually nudging decision latency from 0.33 to 0.52 seconds. For ultra-long tasks spanning tens of minutes or hours, mechanisms will be needed to selectively retrieve and consolidate latent memories rather than holding all historical frames.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation details and real-robot setup
sections.summary: Covers details on teleoperation data collection using the ARX LIFT2 dual-arm mobile robot, prompt formatting for the VLM backbone, and KV cache reuse rates during inference.
sections.details:
### Real-World Robot Platform
Real experiments utilized an ARX LIFT2 dual-arm robot equipped with an omnidirectional mobile base and a lift column. Each arm is a 6-DoF ARX X5. The platform carries three RealSense D405 cameras: one head-mounted and one on each wrist. Demonstration data was gathered via teleoperation using a VR headset and hand controllers. Connected via wired LAN to an inference workstation (RTX 5090 D), the policy outputs 50-step action chunks executed at 30 Hz.

### Prompts and Subtask Annotations
The backbone VLM receives prompts structured as "Front camera: [video] Wrist camera: [current image]", followed by instructions specifying robot constraints and prompting current subtask identification. Subtask labels for real-world tasks were automatically generated using Qwen3-VL followed by manual spot-checking.

### Cache Reuse Details
When applying Efficient Memory CoT Inference, the KV cache prefix hit rate reached 98.4%. Furthermore, the previous subtask was accepted without requiring new autoregressive decoding in 71.2% of decision steps (94% when history was below 60 frames), driving substantial speedups.

takeaways: In memory-augmented VLAs, letting the model reason over what history implies in latent space is far more effective than passing past raw images directly.
Passing subtasks as discrete text strings discards count and progress information, whereas passing hidden states (Latent Memory CoT) retains these critical nuances.
Separating historical reasoning from current perception pathways (Perception Attention) maintains fine-grained manipulation accuracy even when handling long histories.
Because subtasks and history change minimally across consecutive control steps, speculative draft reuse and KV caching dramatically reduce inference latency.
limitations: Retaining all sampled frames within the context causes memory and computation to scale linearly in ultra-long tasks spanning tens of minutes or hours.
Tasks tracking self-exploration history (such as avoiding reopening previously searched drawers) showed lower success rates than external occlusion tasks, leaving room for improvement.
Subtask supervision (manual annotations or VLM auto-segmentation) is required during training, meaning the memory structure is not yet learned completely unsupervised.
